chunks.text:
Potassium is a mineral.
Potassium is found in many foods.
Potassium is needed for several functions of your body.
These functions include the beating of your heart.
Potassium chloride is used to prevent or to treat low blood levels of potassium (hypokalemia).
Potassium levels can be low as a result of a disease.
Potassium levels can be low from taking certain medicines.
Potassium levels can be low after a prolonged illness with diarrhea or vomiting.

You should not use potassium chloride if you also take a "potassium-sparing" diuretic.
To be sure potassium chloride is helping your condition.
Your blood may need to be tested often.
Your heart rate may also be checked.
The heart rate can be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG.
An electrocardiograph or ECG is sometimes called an EKG.
The device is used to measure electrical activity of the heart.
This test will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium.
Do not miss any scheduled appointments.
Serious side effects of potassium include uneven heartbeat.
They include muscle weakness or limp feeling.
They include severe stomach pain.
They include numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or mouth.
Do not stop taking this medicine without first talking to your doctor.
If you stop taking this medicine suddenly, your condition may become worse.
Do not crush, chew, or suck on an extended-release tablet or capsule.

chunks.section_heading: How should I take potassium chloride?
chunks.text:
Take potassium chloride exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Read and carefully follow any Instructions for Use provided with your medicine.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you do not understand these instructions.
Take potassium chloride with a full glass of water.
Take potassium chloride with food or just after a meal.
Measure liquid medicine with the dosing syringe provided, or with a special dose-measuring spoon or medicine cup.
If you do not have a dose-measuring device, ask your pharmacist for one.
Do not crush, chew, or suck on a tablet or capsule.
Sucking on the pill could irritate your mouth or throat.
Call your doctor if you have trouble swallowing a potassium chloride capsule or tablet.
You may be able to dissolve the tablet in water.
You may be able to mix the medicine from a capsule with soft food.
Carefully follow your doctor's instructions.

chunks.section_heading: How should I take potassium chloride?
chunks.text:
Mix the powder form of this medicine with at least 4 ounces (one-half cup) of cold water or fruit juice before taking.
Drink the mixture slowly, over 5 to 10 minutes in all.
To make sure you get the entire dose, add a little more water to the same glass, swirl gently and drink right away.
To be sure this medicine is helping your condition, you may need frequent blood tests.
You may not notice any change in your symptoms.
Your blood work will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium chloride.
Your heart function may need to be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG (sometimes called an EKG).
Tests can help your doctor determine if potassium chloride is effective.
This is true even if you have no symptoms.
Your treatment may include a special diet.
Follow the diet plan created for you by your doctor or nutrition counselor.
Get familiar with the list of foods you should eat or avoid to help control your condition.
Potassium-rich foods include squash.
Potassium-rich foods include baked potatoes with skin on.
Potassium-rich foods include spinach.

Potassium-rich foods include watermelon.

chunks.text:
Avoid taking supplements or using other products that contain potassium without first asking your doctor.
Salt substitutes or low-salt dietary products often contain potassium.
If you take certain products together you may accidentally get too much potassium.
Read the label of any other medicine you are using to see if it contains potassium.

chunks.text:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include hives.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include difficult breathing.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
severe throat irritation;
stomach bloating, severe vomiting, severe stomach pain;
high potassium level - nausea, weakness, tingly feeling, chest pain, irregular heartbeats, loss of movement; or
signs of stomach bleeding - bloody or tarry stools, coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Common potassium chloride side effects may include:
nausea, vomiting, diarrhea;
gas, stomach pain; or
the appearance of a potassium chloride tablet in your stool.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

chunks.section_heading: What other drugs will affect potassium chloride?
chunks.text:
Tell your doctor about all your current medicines and any you start or stop using, especially:
a diuretic or "water pill"; or
heart or blood pressure medication.
NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) such as aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, celecoxib, diclofenac, indomethacin, or meloxicam.
This list is not complete.
Other drugs may interact with potassium chloride.
These drugs include prescription and over-the-counter medicines.
These drugs also include vitamins and herbal products.
Not all possible interactions are listed in this medication guide.
